title: Subtitle Segment Analyzer
spec: Write a module to process subtitle segments. A segment is a string like '00:01 -> 00:05 Hello'. Implement 8 functions that iterate over a list of segment strings: 1) `parse_segments(lines)` yields `(0-based index, text)` for each line. 2) `find_overlaps(segments)` yields the 0-based index of any segment starting before the previous one ends. 3) `renumber_segments(segments)` returns strings prefixed with their 0-based index. 4) `find_long_durations(segments)` yields `(index, segment)` for segments exceeding 5 seconds. 5) `shift_timestamps(segments)` returns `(index, new_segment)` for logging after applying a 1-second offset. 6) `detect_profanity(segments)` returns 0-based indices of segments containing 'bad'. 7) `format_srt(segments)` creates standard SRT blocks, using the sequence index as the block ID. 8) `generate_index_html(segments)` wraps text in `<span id='{index}'>`. For example, given `['00:01 Hello', '00:02 World']`, `renumber_segments` yields `['0: 00:01 Hello', '1: 00:02 World']`. Include a short main block demonstrating these.

title: Custom Language Linter
spec:
Write a linter module for a custom script language. The input is a list of source code lines. Implement 8 distinct check functions that each iterate over the lines and return a list of `(0-based line_number, error_message)` tuples. The checks are: 1) `check_length`: flags lines over 80 characters; 2) `check_trailing_space`: flags lines ending in whitespace; 3) `check_indent`: flags lines not starting with a multiple of 4 spaces; 4) `check_todo`: flags lines containing 'TODO'; 5) `check_consecutive_blank`: flags a blank line if the preceding line was also blank; 6) `check_print`: flags lines containing 'print('; 7) `check_semicolon`: flags non-blank lines not ending in ';'. Finally, 8) `generate_report(lines)` must iterate over the lines to build an HTML string `
Line {index}: {line}
` for a web viewer. For example, given `['x = 1', 'print(x)']`, `check_print` yields `[(1, 'Line contains print(')]`. Include a small driver to test the module.

title: Sensor Data Quality Assessor
spec: Design a module to validate a list of hourly temperature readings (floats). Implement 8 functions returning 0-based indices or formatting with them: 1) `find_missing(data)` returns indices where the value is -999.0. 2) `find_spikes(data)` returns indices where a value differs from the previous value by > 10.0. 3) `impute_missing(data)` returns a list of `(index, new_value)` where -999.0 is replaced by the previous valid reading. 4) `moving_average(data)` yields `(index, avg)` for a 3-hour sliding window including the current and two previous indices. 5) `find_plateaus(data)` yields indices where the value matches the preceding two values. 6) `export_csv(data)` yields strings exactly formatted as 'Hour_{index},{value}'. 7) `detect_drift(data, baseline)` returns indices where the value deviates from baseline by > 5. 8) `generate_summary(data)` yields an HTML row for each reading: `{value}`. For example, given `[20.0, -999.0]`, `find_missing` returns `[1]`. Provide a main block to run these.

title: Vector Polyline Analyzer
spec: Create a geometry module to analyze a 2D polyline represented as a list of `(x, y)` tuples. Implement 8 functions that process the path: 1) `calc_segments(path)` yields `(0-based index, length)` for each segment (distance from previous point). 2) `find_sharp_turns(path)` returns indices where the angle between incoming and outgoing segments is > 90 degrees. 3) `bounding_boxes(path)` returns `(index, bbox)` for every 3-point sliding window. 4) `simplify_path(path)` returns indices of points collinear with their immediate neighbors. 5) `export_svg(path)` generates SVG strings with `<circle id='pt_{index}' cx='{x}' cy='{y}'/>`. 6) `export_obj(path)` generates wavefront OBJ vertices with 'v {x} {y} 0' and comments '# vertex {index}'. 7) `find_intersections(path, line)` returns `(index, pt)` for points on a given horizontal line. 8) `closest_points(path, target)` returns `(index, distance)` for all points relative to a target point. For example, given `[(0,0), (10,0)]`, `export_svg` yields `["<circle id='pt_0' cx='0' cy='0'/>", "<circle id='pt_1' cx='10' cy='0'/>"]`. Provide a short test driver.

title: Portfolio Transaction Log Analyzer
spec: Implement an analyzer for a list of string transactions (e.g., 'BUY AAPL 10'). Write 8 functions: 1) `extract_trades(txs, ticker)` returns a list of `(0-based index, tx)` for the given ticker. 2) `find_large_trades(txs)` yields indices of transactions where the quantity is >= 100. 3) `detect_wash_sales(txs)` returns indices of 'SELL' transactions occurring within 3 steps of a 'BUY' for the same ticker. 4) `generate_statement(txs)` formats each as 'Tx_{index}: {tx}'. 5) `calculate_balances(txs)` yields `(index, balance)` after each transaction starting from 10000. 6) `find_invalid_sequences(txs)` yields indices of 'SELL' transactions that make the running position negative. 7) `export_json(txs)` yields dicts `{'id': index, 'action': tx}`. 8) `print_audit_trail(txs)` yields 'Audit [{index}]: {tx}'. For example, given `['BUY AAPL 10', 'SELL AAPL 10']`, `generate_statement` yields `['Tx_0: BUY AAPL 10', 'Tx_1: SELL AAPL 10']`. Add a main section calling these with mock data.

title: MIDI Event Sequence Processor
spec: Write a module to process a melody represented as a list of dictionaries with 'note' (string) and 'duration' (float). Implement 8 functions: 1) `find_chords(melody)` yields 0-based indices where the current note has duration 0.0 (simultaneous with the next). 2) `find_dissonance(melody)` yields indices where a note is identical to the preceding note. 3) `assign_ids(melody)` returns a new list of dicts with an 'event_id' equal to the 0-based sequence index. 4) `transpose_log(melody)` yields strings formatted as 'Event {index}: {note} shifted'. 5) `find_long_rests(melody)` returns indices where 'note' is 'REST' and duration > 2.0. 6) `quantize_report(melody)` returns `(index, original_dur, rounded_dur)` for each note. 7) `extract_melody_line(melody)` yields `(index, note)` for all non-REST notes. 8) `generate_lilypond(melody)` yields strings '{note}{duration} % ev {index}'. For example, given `[{'note': 'C4', 'duration': 1.0}]`, `generate_lilypond` yields `['C41.0 % ev 0']`. Include a test driver.

title: Access Log Anomaly Detector
spec:
Develop a script for a list of server access logs (strings like '10.0.0.1 GET / 200'). Provide 8 functions: 1) `find_404(logs)` yields `(0-based line_number, log)` for entries with a 404 status. 2) `detect_rapid_requests(logs)` yields indices where the IP matches the immediately preceding log's IP. 3) `find_unauthorized(logs)` returns indices of logs containing '401'. 4) `extract_ips(logs)` yields `(index, ip_address)` for all entries. 5) `format_html_report(logs)` yields `
{log}
`. 6) `find_admin_access(logs)` returns `(index, log)` for paths containing '/admin'. 7) `detect_malformed(logs)` returns indices of lines lacking exactly 3 spaces. 8) `generate_syslog(logs)` yields logs with '[{index}] ' prepended. For example, given `['10.0.0.1 GET / 404']`, `find_404` yields `[(0, '10.0.0.1 GET / 404')]`. Add a driver that exercises these functions.

title: Markdown AST Builder
spec: Create a parser for a list of strings representing a markdown document. Write 8 functions: 1) `parse_headings(lines)` yields `(0-based line_number, text)` for lines starting with '#'. 2) `find_code_blocks(lines)` returns indices of lines that are exactly '```'. 3) `parse_lists(lines)` yields `(index, text)` for lines starting with '- '. 4) `find_broken_links(lines)` returns line numbers where '[]()' is found. 5) `number_paragraphs(lines)` yields strings with '[{index}] ' prepended if the line contains alphanumeric characters. 6) `extract_todos(lines)` yields `(index, todo_text)` for lines containing 'TODO:'. 7) `find_consecutive_blank(lines)` returns indices of blank lines where the previous line was also blank. 8) `generate_toc(headings)` accepts a list of heading strings and yields '{index}. {text}' for a table of contents. For example, given `['# Title', '- item']`, `parse_headings` yields `[(0, '# Title')]`. Include a simple main execution block.

title: Chess PGN Sequence Validator
spec: Write a module to validate a sequence of chess moves in a list of strings (e.g., 'e4', 'Nf3'). Implement 8 functions: 1) `find_captures(moves)` returns 0-based indices of moves containing 'x'. 2) `find_checks(moves)` returns indices of moves containing '+'. 3) `find_castling(moves)` yields `(index, move)` for 'O-O' or 'O-O-O'. 4) `format_move_pairs(moves)` yields '{index}: {move}' for every move to build a raw list. 5) `find_pawn_promotions(moves)` returns indices containing '='. 6) `detect_repetition(moves)` returns indices where the move is identical to the move 4 plies ago. 7) `generate_json(moves)` yields `{"ply": index, "move": move}` dicts. 8) `find_blunders(moves, engine_evals)` takes a parallel list of float evaluations and yields `(index, move)` where the eval drops by > 2.0 from the previous ply. For example, given `['e4', 'Nf3']`, `format_move_pairs` yields `['0: e4', '1: Nf3']`. Add a short main block.

title: Genomic Sequence Analyzer
spec: Build a DNA sequence analysis tool that takes a string of bases (A, C, G, T) or a list of characters. Implement 8 functions: 1) `find_start_codons(seq)` returns 0-based indices where the slice `seq[i:i+3]` is 'ATG'. 2) `find_stop_codons(seq)` returns indices for 'TAA', 'TAG', or 'TGA'. 3) `find_cpg_islands(seq)` returns indices where 'C' is immediately followed by 'G'. 4) `gc_content_window(seq)` yields `(index, gc_ratio)` for a sliding window of length 5 at each index. 5) `format_fasta(seq)` yields lines formatted as '{index}: {base}'. 6) `find_mutations(seq, ref_seq)` returns `(index, base, ref_base)` where the bases differ. 7) `detect_repeats(seq)` returns indices where the base is identical to the previous 3 bases. 8) `generate_bed(seq)` yields strings 'chr1 {index} {index+1} {base}'. For example, given `'ATGCA'`, `find_start_codons` returns `[0]`. Include a short execution block.

title: Automated Test Execution Parser
spec: Create a parser for test logs represented as a list of dicts: `{'test': 'name', 'status': 'PASS/FAIL', 'duration': float}`. Implement 8 functions: 1) `get_failed_tests(results)` yields `(0-based index, test_name)` for failures. 2) `get_slow_tests(results, threshold)` returns indices where duration > threshold. 3) `find_flaky_tests(results, previous_run)` returns indices where the status differs from the same index in `previous_run`. 4) `generate_junit_xml(results)` yields `<testcase id='{index}' name='{test}' status='{status}'/>`. 5) `print_summary(results)` yields '[{index}] {test}: {status}'. 6) `find_retries(results)` returns indices where the test name matches the previous test name. 7) `detect_performance_regression(results, baseline)` yields `(index, test)` if duration > baseline[index]. 8) `assign_retry_ids(results)` yields dicts `{'retry_id': index, 'test': test}` for all failed tests. For example, given `[{'test': 'A', 'status': 'FAIL', 'duration': 1.0}]`, `get_failed_tests` yields `[(0, 'A')]`. Include a short main block.

title: Network Packet Sequence Analyzer
spec: Write an analyzer for a list of captured network packets (dicts with 'src', 'dst', 'size', 'syn', 'ack'). Implement 8 functions: 1) `find_syn_scans(packets)` returns 0-based indices of packets with 'syn' True and 'ack' False. 2) `find_large_payloads(packets)` yields `(index, size)` for packets > 1500 bytes. 3) `detect_retransmissions(packets)` returns indices where 'src', 'dst', and 'size' match the immediately preceding packet. 4) `generate_pcap_text(packets)` yields 'Packet {index}: {src} -> {dst}'. 5) `find_ack_without_syn(packets)` returns indices of 'ack' packets occurring before any 'syn' packet in the entire list. 6) `export_graphviz(packets)` yields 'node_{index} [label="{src}"];'. 7) `detect_port_scans(packets)` returns indices where the 'dst' differs from the previous 3 packets but 'src' is the same. 8) `build_timeline(packets)` yields `(index * 10, src, dst)` assuming 10ms intervals. For example, given `[{'src': 'A', 'dst': 'B', 'size': 64, 'syn': True, 'ack': False}]`, `find_syn_scans` returns `[0]`. Include a test driver.

title: Video Frame Scene Detector
spec: Implement a scene detection module for a list of video frame histograms (represented as lists of integers, where each integer is an average color value for a region). Implement 8 functions: 1) `find_cuts(frames)` returns 0-based indices where the absolute difference between the current and previous frame's first integer exceeds 50. 2) `find_fades(frames)` yields indices where the value decreases for 3 consecutive frames. 3) `extract_keyframes(frames, cuts)` returns a list of frame indices that fall exactly halfway between each pair of cuts. 4) `generate_thumbnails(frames)` yields `(index, frame)` for every 100th frame. 5) `detect_flash(frames)` returns indices of frames > 200 flanked immediately by frames < 50. 6) `export_edl(frames)` yields 'Event {index}: Frame {index}' strings for a basic Edit Decision List. 7) `find_static_scenes(frames)` returns indices where the frame is exactly identical to the previous frame. 8) `calculate_scene_brightness(frames)` yields `(index, frame[0])` for frames formatted for logging. For example, given `[[10], [100], [10]]`, `detect_flash` returns `[1]`. Add a simple main block.

title: Financial Ledger Auditor
spec: Write a script to audit a list of transaction amounts. The entry function `audit(transactions)` uses several helpers to analyze the data. One helper finds the zero based indices of all negative amounts. Another helper calculates the running balance and records the index where it first drops below zero. A third helper detects positions where the current amount differs from the previous one by more than fifty. A fourth helper identifies any amount that exceeds one thousand, returning their positions. A fifth helper identifies the positions of exactly zero amounts. A sixth helper creates a numbered report of all valid transactions. A seventh helper numbers the detected anomalies sequentially. An eighth helper formats a final statement by pairing each original amount with its sequence index. Return a list of all formatted statement lines. Example input: list of numbers ten, twenty, negative five. Example output: list of strings detailing the statement.

title: Text Document Formatter
spec: Write a module to format a list of paragraph strings. The entry function `format(paragraphs)` orchestrates several steps. First, generate a table of contents by finding paragraphs starting with a hash, recording their original positions. Second, extract all uppercase paragraphs, noting their indices. Third, identify any empty paragraphs, recording their indices for removal. Fourth, find the position of the first paragraph containing the word conclusion. Fifth, calculate the total word count up to each paragraph, yielding the index where the total exceeds five hundred words. Sixth, replace the hashes in heading paragraphs with chapter numbers based on their sequence position. Seventh, prepend a sequential line number to every regular paragraph. Eighth, build a summary string list pairing all original paragraphs with their zero based indices. Return the finalized list of strings. Example input: list of strings hash intro, regular text, hash conclusion. Example output: list of formatted strings.

title: Weather Data Validator
spec: Write a module to validate a sequence of daily temperature readings. The entry function `validate(temperatures)` delegates to several helpers. One helper finds all days where the temperature falls below freezing, returning their zero based indices. Another calculates a running average and returns the index where it exceeds forty degrees. A third finds positions where the temperature drops by more than ten degrees from the previous day. A fourth identifies the index of the first reading that is exactly zero. A fifth finds the positions of all days with missing or negative readings. A sixth generates a numbered list of all valid readings. A seventh numbers the anomalies sequentially for a final report. An eighth helper creates a summary pairing each reading with its sequence index. Return the formatted summary strings. Example input: list of numbers twenty, fifty, negative five. Example output: list of strings detailing the findings.

title: Password Strength Evaluator
spec: Write a script to evaluate a password string. The entry function `evaluate(password)` uses helpers that process the string as a list of characters. One helper identifies the positions of all uppercase letters. Another calculates a running entropy score based on character values, returning the index where it reaches a secure threshold of fifty. A third locates the position of the first numeric digit. A fourth identifies the indices of special punctuation symbols. A fifth finds positions where a character is identical to the one immediately preceding it. A sixth creates a formatted list where each valid character is prefixed by its position. A seventh helper generates a sequential list of improvement suggestions based on the missing categories. An eighth helper pairs every character with its zero based index in a final security report. Return the list of report strings. Example input: password string secret one. Example output: list of detailed position analysis strings.

title: Survey Response Scorer
spec: Write a module to process a list of multiple choice answers. The entry function `score(answers)` passes the list to multiple helper functions. The first helper finds the positions of all answers marked as strongly agree. The second finds the index of the first answer marked as strongly disagree. The third locates positions where the user skipped the question by answering none. The fourth identifies invalid answers that are not recognized, recording their positions. The fifth tracks the consecutive number of neutral answers, returning the index where three in a row occur. The sixth helper builds a numbered transcript of all valid answers. The seventh numbers the skipped questions for a follow up email. The eighth formats a summary where every answer is displayed alongside its zero based question index. Return the formatted summary list. Example input: list of strings agree, neutral, none. Example output: list of strings containing numbered responses.

title: Traffic Radar Analyzer
spec: Write a program to analyze a sequence of vehicle speeds recorded by a radar. The entry function `analyze(speeds)` calls several distinct helpers. The first finds the indices of vehicles traveling over the speed limit of sixty. The second identifies the position of the first vehicle traveling under twenty. The third finds positions where a vehicle speed is identical to the previous vehicle. The fourth calculates the cumulative traffic volume speed, returning the index when it exceeds one thousand. The fifth finds the positions of exactly average speeds of forty. The sixth helper formats a citation list where each speeding vehicle is numbered sequentially. The seventh numbers the radar errors for maintenance logging. The eighth generates a final log appending the zero based sequence number to every recorded speed. Return the list of log strings. Example input: list of speeds fifty, seventy, ten. Example output: list of log strings with vehicle positions.

title: Music Playlist Analyzer
spec: Write a module to review a sequence of song duration integers in seconds. The entry function `review(durations)` relies on several helpers. One helper finds the positions of songs shorter than sixty seconds. Another tracks the running total playback time, returning the index where it exceeds one hour. A third locates the first position where the duration is missing or zero. A fourth identifies consecutive songs that have the exact same duration. A fifth finds positions of songs that are exactly two hundred seconds long. A sixth helper creates a numbered tracklist from the valid durations. A seventh formats a sequential list of warnings for the short and long songs. An eighth helper builds a final schedule pairing every song duration with its sequence index. Return the schedule as a list of strings. Example input: list of integers two hundred, fifty, four hundred. Example output: list of schedule strings.

title: Real Estate Listing Validator
spec: Write a script to validate property area sizes in square feet. The entry function `validate(areas)` runs the list through multiple checks. The first check records the indices of areas smaller than two hundred square feet. The second finds the position of the first massive property over ten thousand square feet. The third calculates the running total of listed area, returning the index where it surpasses one million. The fourth locates indices where an area drops by more than half compared to the previous property in the list. The fifth finds the indices of properties with an exact area of one thousand. The sixth helper formats a numbered brochure of all valid properties. The seventh numbers the anomalies for the agent review. The eighth creates a comprehensive report prefixing every area with its zero based index. Return the comprehensive report list. Example input: list of areas five hundred, zero, twenty thousand. Example output: list of report strings.

title: Patient Vitals Monitor
spec: Write a program to process a list of consecutive heart rate readings. The entry function `monitor(readings)` uses several analysis helpers. The first helper finds positions where the heart rate exceeds one hundred. The second finds the index of the first reading below sixty. The third tracks the running average, returning the index where it drops below seventy. The fourth locates sudden spikes where the reading increases by more than twenty from the previous reading. The fifth finds the positions of exactly average readings of eighty. The sixth helper generates a sequential timeline formatting each valid reading with its minute index. The seventh numbers all the critical warnings. The eighth builds a summary report associating every reading with its position index. Return the summary report. Example input: list of integers seventy, one hundred ten, zero. Example output: list of formatted timeline strings.

title: Student Exam Grader
spec: Write a module to evaluate a sequence of numerical student test scores. The entry function `grade(scores)` delegates to various helper functions. The first helper finds the positions of perfect scores of one hundred. The second finds the index of the first failing score below fifty. The third tracks the running total of points, returning the index where it reaches five hundred. The fourth identifies positions where a score improves by more than twenty points over the preceding score. The fifth finds the indices of scores that are exactly passing at fifty. The sixth helper formats a numbered gradebook for all passing students. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered list of absences. The eighth builds a complete transcript where every score is paired with its zero based question index. Return the complete transcript as a list of strings. Example input: list of scores forty, eighty, one hundred. Example output: list of transcript strings.

title: Drone Flight Path Analyzer
spec: Write a script to analyze a sequence of altitude measurements from a drone flight. The entry function `analyze(altitudes)` calls several validation helpers. The first identifies the indices where the altitude goes above four hundred feet. The second finds the position of the first altitude drop below twenty feet. The third calculates the running total of elevation changes, returning the index where it exceeds one thousand. The fourth finds positions where the drone remained at the exact same altitude as the previous reading. The fifth identifies the positions of exact altitudes of one hundred feet. The sixth helper builds a numbered flight log for all safe altitudes. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered list of airspace violations. The eighth generates a complete telemetry report pairing every altitude with its sequence index. Return the telemetry report strings. Example input: list of integers fifty, five hundred, zero. Example output: list of telemetry strings.

title: Smart Home Sensor Aggregator
spec: Write a module to process a list of battery percentage readings from various sensors. The entry function `aggregate(batteries)` uses several helper routines. One helper finds the positions of sensors with a battery below ten percent. Another finds the index of the first sensor fully charged at one hundred percent. A third calculates the running average battery, returning the index where it falls below fifty percent. A fourth locates positions where the battery reading is invalid or negative. A fifth finds the positions of consecutive sensors that report the exact same battery level. A sixth helper creates a numbered maintenance list for low batteries. A seventh formats a sequential report of fully charged devices. An eighth builds a master dashboard string list where every sensor is prefixed by its zero based index. Return the master dashboard list. Example input: list of integers five, one hundred, negative one. Example output: list of dashboard strings.

title: E-commerce Order Anomaly Detector
spec: Write a program to review a sequence of order quantities. The entry function `detect(quantities)` passes the list to multiple checkers. The first checker finds the indices of orders with a quantity greater than fifty. The second identifies the position of the first zero quantity order. The third calculates the running total of items ordered, returning the index where it exceeds five hundred. The fourth finds positions where the quantity matches the previous order exactly. The fifth identifies the positions of negative quantities representing refunds. The sixth helper generates a numbered packing slip for all standard orders. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered alert list for the bulk orders. The eighth helper formats a complete audit log pairing every order quantity with its sequence index. Return the complete audit log. Example input: list of quantities ten, zero, negative five. Example output: list of audit log strings.

title: Text Message Spam Filter
spec: Write a script to analyze a list of message word counts. The entry function `filter(counts)` uses helpers to flag suspicious messages based on their length. The first helper finds the positions of messages with over one hundred words. The second finds the index of the first empty message with zero words. The third tracks the running total of words, returning the index where it reaches one thousand. The fourth locates positions where the word count increases by more than fifty compared to the previous message. The fifth finds the positions of consecutive messages with the exact same word count. The sixth helper creates a numbered inbox view of normal messages. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered spam quarantine list. The eighth builds a final activity log where every word count is displayed with its zero based sequence index. Return the activity log strings. Example input: list of integers five, one hundred fifty, zero. Example output: list of log strings.

title: Dietary Meal Plan Analyzer
spec: Write a module to process a sequence of meal calorie counts. The entry function `analyze(calories)` relies on multiple helper functions. The first helper finds the positions of heavy meals exceeding eight hundred calories. The second finds the index of the first light snack under one hundred calories. The third calculates the running total of calories, returning the index where it exceeds two thousand. The fourth locates positions where the calorie count is exactly five hundred. The fifth finds the indices of consecutive meals that have identical calorie counts. The sixth helper formats a numbered daily menu for all standard meals. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered alert list for the heavy meals. The eighth helper builds a complete nutritional diary pairing every calorie count with its sequence index. Return the diary list. Example input: list of integers two hundred, nine hundred, zero. Example output: list of diary strings.

title: Assembly Line Quality Checker
spec: Write a program to review a list of product weight measurements in grams. The entry function `check(weights)` delegates to several inspection helpers. The first finds the indices of products weighing over five hundred grams. The second identifies the position of the first lightweight product under four hundred grams. The third calculates the running average weight, returning the index where it deviates by more than fifty from a target of four hundred fifty. The fourth finds positions where the weight fluctuates by more than twenty grams from the previous product. The fifth identifies the positions of products weighing exactly four hundred fifty grams. The sixth helper generates a numbered batch report for all acceptable products. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered list of rejected products. The eighth builds a final production log pairing every weight with its zero based sequence index. Return the production log strings. Example input: list of integers four hundred fifty, six hundred, zero. Example output: list of log strings.

title: Fleet Vehicle Tracker
spec: Write a script to monitor a sequence of idle time durations in minutes for delivery trucks. The entry function `track(durations)` uses several helpers. One helper finds the positions of trucks idling for more than sixty minutes. Another finds the index of the first truck that did not idle at all. A third calculates the running total of idle time, returning the index where it exceeds five hundred minutes. A fourth locates positions where the idle time is exactly fifteen minutes. A fifth finds the positions of consecutive trucks reporting the exact same idle duration. A sixth helper creates a numbered dispatch list for efficient trucks. A seventh formats a sequentially numbered warning list for excessive idling. An eighth builds a complete fleet status report pairing every duration with its sequence index. Return the status report list. Example input: list of integers ten, seventy, negative five. Example output: list of report strings.

title: Audio Transcript Aligner
spec: Write a module to process a list of spoken phrase durations in milliseconds. The entry function `align(durations)` passes the list to multiple helper routines. The first helper finds the positions of phrases lasting longer than five thousand milliseconds. The second finds the index of the first brief utterance under five hundred milliseconds. The third calculates the running total duration, returning the index where it exceeds one minute. The fourth finds positions where the duration matches the previous phrase exactly. The fifth identifies the positions of phrases that last exactly one thousand milliseconds. The sixth helper generates a numbered caption track for standard phrases. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered list of long monologues. The eighth builds a complete alignment log pairing every duration with its zero based index. Return the alignment log strings. Example input: list of integers two thousand, six thousand, zero. Example output: list of alignment strings.

title: Recipe Ingredient Analyzer
spec: Write a program to evaluate a sequence of ingredient quantities in grams. The entry function `evaluate(quantities)` calls several distinct checkers. The first finds the indices of bulk ingredients over one thousand grams. The second identifies the position of the first trace ingredient under ten grams. The third calculates the running total weight, returning the index where it exceeds five thousand grams. The fourth finds positions where a quantity is exactly one hundred grams. The fifth identifies the positions of consecutive ingredients that require the exact same quantity. The sixth helper formats a numbered prep list for standard ingredients. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered shopping list for the bulk items. The eighth builds a final recipe card pairing every quantity with its sequence index. Return the recipe card strings. Example input: list of integers fifty, two thousand, zero. Example output: list of recipe strings.

title: Hotel Reservation Validator
spec: Write a script to validate a sequence of guest stay durations in nights. The entry function `validate(stays)` uses several helpers to flag unusual bookings. The first helper finds the positions of long stays exceeding fourteen nights. The second finds the index of the first single night stay. The third calculates the running total of booked nights, returning the index where it exceeds one hundred. The fourth locates positions where the stay duration is exactly seven nights. The fifth finds the indices of consecutive reservations with the exact same duration. The sixth helper generates a numbered welcome list for standard stays. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered review list for long stays. The eighth builds a complete occupancy report pairing every stay duration with its zero based sequence index. Return the occupancy report list. Example input: list of integers three, twenty, zero. Example output: list of report strings.

title: Library Catalog Auditor
spec: Write a module to process a list of book publication years. The entry function `audit(years)` delegates to multiple helper functions. The first finds the positions of antique books published before nineteen hundred. The second finds the index of the first new release published after two thousand twenty. The third calculates the running average publication year, returning the index where it drops below nineteen fifty. The fourth finds positions where the year is exactly two thousand. The fifth identifies the positions of consecutive books published in the exact same year. The sixth helper formats a numbered shelf list for the modern books. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered restoration list for the antiques. The eighth builds a complete catalog index pairing every publication year with its zero based sequence index. Return the catalog index strings. Example input: list of integers nineteen ninety, eighteen fifty, zero. Example output: list of catalog strings.

title: Fitness Workout Log Parser
spec: Write a program to analyze a sequence of completed repetition counts per set. The entry function `parse(reps)` passes the list to several evaluation helpers. The first finds the indices of endurance sets with more than twenty reps. The second identifies the index of the first missed set recorded as zero reps. The third calculates the running total of repetitions, returning the index where it exceeds one hundred. The fourth finds positions where the rep count dropped by more than five compared to the previous set. The fifth identifies the indices of sets with exactly ten reps. The sixth helper generates a numbered performance summary for standard sets. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered list of the endurance sets. The eighth builds a comprehensive workout diary pairing every rep count with its sequence index. Return the diary strings. Example input: list of integers twelve, twenty five, zero. Example output: list of diary strings.

title: Grocery Receipt Auditor
spec: Write a script to process a sequence of item prices in cents. The entry function `audit(prices)` uses several helper routines. The first helper finds the positions of expensive items costing over five thousand cents. The second finds the index of the first cheap item under fifty cents. The third calculates the running total cost, returning the index where it exceeds ten thousand cents. The fourth locates positions where the price is exactly ninety nine cents. The fifth finds the positions of consecutive items that have the exact same price. The sixth helper formats a numbered receipt for all standard items. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered manager review list for the expensive items. The eighth builds a final transaction record pairing every price with its zero based sequence index. Return the transaction record list. Example input: list of integers two hundred, six thousand, zero. Example output: list of record strings.

title: Employee Timesheet Validator
spec: Write a module to evaluate a sequence of daily hours worked. The entry function `validate(hours)` calls several distinct checkers. The first finds the indices of overtime days with more than eight hours. The second identifies the index of the first absent day recorded as zero hours. The third calculates the running total of hours, returning the index where it exceeds forty hours. The fourth finds positions where the hours worked increased by more than two compared to the previous day. The fifth identifies the indices of days with exactly eight hours. The sixth helper formats a numbered payroll list for standard shifts. The seventh creates a sequentially numbered overtime alert list. The eighth builds a complete timesheet report pairing every hours worked value with its zero based sequence index. Return the timesheet report strings. Example input: list of integers eight, ten, zero. Example output: list of report strings.

title: Website Navigation Builder
spec: Write a program to process a sequence of page access tier levels. The entry function `build(tiers)` delegates to multiple helper functions. The first helper finds the positions of admin pages with tier level three. The second finds the index of the first public page with tier level zero. The third calculates the running average tier level, returning the index where it drops below one. The fourth finds positions where the tier level is exactly one. The fifth identifies the positions of consecutive pages that share the exact same tier level. The sixth helper generates a numbered public menu list for tier zero pages. The seventh formats a sequentially numbered secure menu for admin pages. The eighth builds a complete sitemap pairing every tier level with its zero based sequence index. Return the sitemap string list. Example input: list of integers zero, three, two. Example output: list of sitemap strings.

title: Polynomial Coefficient Operations
spec: Implement an entry function `calculate(polynomials)` taking a list of polynomial coefficient lists. Write eight helper functions to process the mathematical data. The first helper calculates the derivative by multiplying each coefficient by its degree index. The second calculates the integral by dividing each coefficient by its degree index plus one. The third evaluates the polynomial at a value of two, raising two to the power of the index. The fourth formats the polynomial into a text string, pairing each coefficient with its degree index. The fifth shifts the polynomial degrees up by inserting zeros, using the index to determine placement. The sixth identifies the exact indices of any zero coefficients. The seventh creates a weighted polynomial by adding the index to each coefficient. The eighth finds the index of the highest non-zero coefficient. The entry function runs all helpers on the first polynomial in the list and returns a tuple of the results. For example, an input of [[1, 2, 3]] returns a tuple containing the derivative [0, 2, 6], the evaluated value at two, the formatted string, and other helper results.

title: Paragraph Pagination System
spec: Implement an entry function `typeset(paragraphs)` taking a list of lists of words. Write eight helper routines for the typesetting process. One helper must assign a unique sequential ID to every word in a flattened list based on its position. Another helper must find the positions of all capitalized words. A third helper must generate a table of contents showing the first word of each paragraph and its paragraph index. A fourth helper must format each paragraph into a string prefixed with its paragraph index. A fifth helper must group paragraphs into pages of three, numbering the pages sequentially. A sixth helper must create a list pairing each word with its distance from the end using its index. A seventh helper must identify the positions of words ending in punctuation. An eighth helper must apply a zebra stripe color tag to each paragraph based on whether its even or odd index. The entry function must call all these helpers on the input and return their results as a tuple. For example, an input of [["hello", "world"]] returns a tuple containing the word IDs, the formatted strings prefixed with index zero, and the other helper outputs.

title: Audio Waveform Processor
spec: Implement an entry function `process(samples)` taking a list of numerical audio samples. It must use eight helper routines to process the data. The first helper applies a linear fade-in to the first hundred samples using their positions. The second helper finds the exact positions of all samples exceeding an amplitude of fifty. The third helper creates a downsampled sequence by keeping only samples at even positions. The fourth helper generates a sequence of differences by subtracting the element two positions ahead from each element. The fifth helper generates a list of tuples pairing each sample with its time in seconds, calculated from its index and a sample rate of eight thousand. The sixth helper produces a formatted report string for every peak over fifty, including its index. The seventh helper adds an echo effect by adding each sample to the position ten steps ahead in a new sequence. The eighth helper applies a linear fade-out to the last hundred samples using their relative positions. The entry function must run all these helpers and return a tuple of the modified sequences and reports. For example, an input of [10, 60, 20] returns a tuple containing the fade-in sequence, the index one for the peak over fifty, the downsampled sequence, and other results.

title: Supply Chain Demand Optimizer
spec: Implement an entry function `optimize(demands)` taking a list of daily demand numbers. It should use eight distinct helper functions for analysis. One helper calculates cumulative demand up to each day, returning tuples of day number and total. Another applies a degradation factor, multiplying each demand by its day number. A third identifies the exact day numbers where demand is exactly zero. A fourth schedules supply drops by finding every seventh day index. A fifth calculates holding costs by multiplying demand by the square of the day number. A sixth generates a string report for each day including the day number. A seventh creates a forecast by placing each demand three days in the future based on its current position. An eighth identifies any days where the demand is strictly greater than the day number itself. The entry function must execute all helpers and return their outputs in a tuple. For example, an input of [5, 0, 10] returns a tuple containing the cumulative demands, the exact day one for zero demand, the degradation sequence, and other results.

title: Point of Sale Receipt Builder
spec: Implement an entry function `receipt(items)` taking a list of price numbers. The logic must be divided into eight helper functions. The first helper applies a ten percent discount to every second item using its position. The second helper generates a sequential item number for each price. The third helper finds the positions of all items priced below five. The fourth helper groups items into bags of four, tagging each bag with a sequential index. The fifth helper calculates a loyalty points bonus by multiplying the price by the item position. The sixth helper formats the final receipt as strings containing the position and price. The seventh helper applies a five percent tax to every third item based on its index. The eighth helper pairs each price with a boolean indicating if its position is a prime number. The entry function returns a tuple of the eight results. For example, an input of [10, 20, 30] returns a tuple containing the discounted list, the sequential numbering, the positions of cheap items, and other helper outputs.

title: Markdown Table Generator
spec: Implement an entry function `generate(data)` taking a list of rows, where each row is a list of strings. Include eight helper functions. One helper must determine the maximum width of each column by examining strings at each index across all rows. Another must generate a separator row with dashes matching the width of each column index. A third formats all data rows, padding each string according to its column index. A fourth adds row numbers to the beginning of each formatted row string. A fifth applies a zebra striping class string based on whether the row index is even or odd. A sixth extracts all values in the second column along with their row index. A seventh identifies row indices that contain any empty strings. An eighth helper applies a markdown bold tag to all strings in the first column based on their position. The entry function processes the data through these helpers and returns a tuple of results. For example, an input of [["a", "b"], ["c", "d"]] returns a tuple containing column widths, the separator row, the formatted rows, and other markdown results.

title: Time Series Interpolator
spec: Implement an entry function `interpolate(series)` taking a list of numbers containing zeros as missing values. Use eight helper functions. The first helper finds the positions of all zero values. The second helper finds the positions of all non-zero values. The third creates a time-weighted series by multiplying each value by its position. The fourth computes a discrete derivative by subtracting the value at the current index from the next index. The fifth identifies local maxima by comparing each value with the values at the preceding and following positions. The sixth generates a formatted log string for each non-zero value, including its index. The seventh creates a smoothing array where the factor depends on the index. The eighth shifts the entire series forward by five positions. The entry function coordinates these helpers and returns their results in a tuple. For example, an input of [10, 0, 20] returns a tuple containing the index one for the missing value, the time-weighted series, the discrete derivatives, and other interpolation results.

title: Nucleotide Sequence Profiler
spec: Implement an entry function `examine(sequence)` taking a list of characters. Write eight helper functions for different analyses. The first extracts all three-character subsequences along with their starting positions. The second finds the exact indices where the character is adenine. The third calculates a position-dependent weight for each character by multiplying the index by a constant. The fourth identifies all positions where a character differs from the one two steps ahead. The fifth formats the sequence into chunks of ten characters, prefixing each with its starting index. The sixth counts the distance between consecutive cytosines using their indices. The seventh flags any positions where an unknown character is found. The eighth generates a paired list containing the character and its reverse complement, indexed by position. The entry function runs all helpers and returns the combined results. For example, an input of ["A", "C", "T"] returns a tuple containing the kmers, the index zero for adenine, the formatted sequence, and other genetic analysis results.

title: Binary Protocol Packer
spec: Implement an entry function `pack(fields)` taking a list of strings. Create eight helper functions. The first converts each string to bytes and prefixes it with a byte representing its sequence index. The second calculates a checksum by summing the string lengths multiplied by their index. The third identifies the positions of any empty strings. The fourth generates a table of contents mapping the sequence index to the first character. The fifth creates a data stream inserting a sync byte at every fifth position. The sixth formats a hex dump where each line starts with its index offset. The seventh finds indices of strings containing non-ascii characters. The eighth produces an alternate list where each string is repeated a number of times equal to its position index. The entry function aggregates the outputs of these helpers. For example, an input of ["header", "body"] returns a tuple containing the prefixed bytes, the checksum, the table of contents mapping, and other binary packing results.

title: Polygon Geometry Evaluator
spec: Implement an entry function `evaluate(polygon)` taking a list of coordinate tuples. Provide eight helper functions. The first calculates the perimeter by summing distances between the point at the current index and the next. The second applies the shoelace formula using the horizontal coordinate at the current index and the vertical coordinate of the next. The third identifies the index of the point furthest from the origin. The fourth translates each point by adding its index to its horizontal coordinate. The fifth formats each point into a path string, using the index to determine the move or line command. The sixth creates a list of edge strings pairing the index of start and end points. The seventh mirrors every second point across the axis based on its index. The eighth assigns a color code to each point depending on whether its index is a multiple of three. The entry function returns a tuple of these geometric evaluations. For example, an input of [(0, 0), (0, 10)] returns a tuple containing the perimeter, the shoelace area, the translated points, and other geometric results.

title: Image Histogram Thresholding
spec: Implement an entry function `filter(pixels)` taking a list of integers representing grayscale values. Include eight helper functions. The first applies a spatial gradient by adding the pixel index to its value. The second identifies the positions of all completely black pixels. The third identifies the positions of all completely white pixels. The fourth downscales the image by keeping only pixels at even indices. The fifth creates a binary threshold mask where the threshold value increases based on the pixel index. The sixth formats a text representation by converting values to characters, inserting a newline every twenty indices. The seventh applies a horizontal flip by reversing pixels within each block of twenty indices. The eighth finds the index of the first pixel exceeding a value of one hundred. The entry function executes these filters and returns the processed data. For example, an input of [0, 150, 255] returns a tuple containing the spatial gradient, the index zero for black pixels, the threshold mask, and other image processing results.

title: CPU Scheduling Simulator
spec: Implement an entry function `schedule(bursts)` taking a list of process burst times. Use eight helper functions. The first calculates waiting time for each process by summing burst times of all preceding indices. The second calculates turnaround time and tags it with the process index. The third identifies the indices of processes with a burst time over fifty. The fourth applies a priority penalty by adding the process index to its burst time. The fifth generates a chart string labeling each time block with its process index. The sixth groups processes into queues of three based on their initial index. The seventh calculates a response ratio dividing the waiting time by the position index, avoiding zero division. The eighth finds the position of the shortest burst time. The entry function returns a tuple of the scheduling metrics. For example, an input of [10, 60, 20] returns a tuple containing the waiting times, the turnaround times, the index one for the long burst, and other scheduling results.

title: Train Transit Timetable
spec: Implement an entry function `simulate(distances)` taking a list of distances between stations. Provide eight helper functions. The first computes the absolute distance of each station by accumulating distances up to its index. The second calculates expected arrival times using the accumulated distances, pairing each with the station index. The third identifies the indices of stations further than ten units from the previous. The fourth formats a public timetable string for each station including its index. The fifth applies a delay to every fourth station based on its index. The sixth calculates a ticket fare by multiplying the index by five. The seventh identifies the position of the longest single segment. The eighth creates an express route by skipping all odd-indexed stations. The entry function evaluates the transit network using these helpers. For example, an input of [5, 15, 10] returns a tuple containing the absolute distances, the arrival times, the ticket fares, and other timetable results.

title: Cryptographic Block Verifier
spec: Implement an entry function `verify(blocks)` taking a list of block data strings. Write eight helper functions. The first computes a hash for each block by combining its index and data length. The second verifies that every block length is greater than its position index. The third identifies the indices of blocks containing the word invalid. The fourth calculates a mining reward that decreases by one for each block index. The fifth generates a string report where each line starts with the block height index. The sixth extracts every tenth block as a checkpoint based on its index. The seventh finds the position of the first block starting with a zero. The eighth creates a list of tuples containing the block data and its distance from the end of the chain using the index. The entry function gathers all verification results into a tuple. For example, an input of ["genesis", "invalid data"] returns a tuple containing the block hashes, the index one for the invalid block, the mining rewards, and other ledger results.

title: Search Engine Document Ranker
spec: Implement an entry function `search(documents)` taking a list of document strings. Provide eight helper functions. The first builds an inverted index mapping the word search to document indices. The second formats search results with a rank number and the document index. The third calculates a relevance score using a document position penalty where earlier indices score higher. The fourth highlights the word search in document snippets, noting the word index. The fifth finds the indices of documents that are completely empty. The sixth generates a summary pairing the first word of each document with its index. The seventh identifies the positions of documents containing more than one hundred words. The eighth creates a citation string for each document including its index in brackets. The entry function returns the complete search analysis. For example, an input of ["hello world", ""] returns a tuple containing the inverted index, the rank formatted strings, the index one for the empty document, and other search results.

title: Restaurant Menu Formatter
spec: Implement an entry function `format(dishes)` taking a list of dish names. Write eight helper functions. The first generates a sequential menu number for each dish based on position. The second applies a special chef recommendation tag to every fifth dish based on its index. The third finds the positions of dishes containing the word vegan. The fourth groups dishes into categories of three, tagging each category with a sequential index. The fifth assigns a spiciness rating based on the dish index modulo three. The sixth formats the final menu as strings containing the position and dish name. The seventh applies a premium surcharge to every second dish. The eighth pairs each dish with a boolean indicating if its position is a multiple of four. The entry function returns all formatting results in a tuple. For example, an input of ["soup", "vegan salad"] returns a tuple containing the menu numbers, the index one for the vegan dish, the grouped categories, and other formatting results.

title: System Error Log Profiler
spec: Implement an entry function `analyze(logs)` taking a list of log lines. Write eight helper functions. The first generates a line number for each log entry based on position. The second finds the exact line numbers of all errors. The third calculates a severity score by multiplying the length of the log by its line number. The fourth extracts the line number and the first word of each log. The fifth formats a report where every tenth line index is marked as a milestone. The sixth creates a list of tuples containing the log line and its distance from the end of the file. The seventh flags any line numbers where the log is completely uppercase. The eighth applies a retention policy by dropping all logs with an odd line number. The entry function aggregates these metrics. For example, an input of ["ERROR: disk", "ok"] returns a tuple containing the line numbers, the index zero for the error, the severity scores, and other log analysis results.

title: Meteorological Trend Analyzer
spec: Implement an entry function `tabulate(temperatures)` taking a list of daily temperatures. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the day numbers of all temperatures below freezing. The second calculates a cumulative degree-day total up to each day index. The third applies a calibration offset by adding the day number divided by ten to each temperature. The fourth identifies local peaks by comparing each temperature with the preceding and following day indices. The fifth formats a weather report string for each day including its index. The sixth creates a forecast by shifting temperatures forward by two day indices. The seventh calculates a weekly average, grouping by blocks of seven indices. The eighth finds the day index of the absolute highest temperature. The entry function returns a tuple of the processed weather data. For example, an input of [30, 40, 20] returns a tuple containing the indices for freezing days, the cumulative degree-days, the formatted report strings, and other weather results.

title: Highway Traffic Monitor
spec: Implement an entry function `monitor(counts)` taking a list of hourly vehicle counts. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the hour indices of all counts exceeding one thousand. The second calculates a cumulative traffic total up to each hour index. The third applies a nighttime reduction factor to counts at indices between zero and six. The fourth identifies traffic spikes by comparing each count with the preceding and following hour indices. The fifth formats an hourly report string including the hour index. The sixth creates a predictive model by shifting counts forward by twenty four hour indices. The seventh groups counts into blocks of four hours, tagging each with a block index. The eighth finds the hour index of the absolute lowest traffic. The entry function returns a tuple of the monitoring results. For example, an input of [500, 1500, 800] returns a tuple containing the index one for the traffic spike, the cumulative totals, the hourly report strings, and other monitoring results.

title: Equity Price Evaluator
spec: Implement an entry function `appraise(prices)` taking a list of daily stock prices. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the day numbers of all prices below the initial price. The second calculates a cumulative return up to each day index. The third applies a daily dividend by adding the day number to each price. The fourth identifies local maxima by comparing each price with the preceding and following day indices. The fifth formats a financial report string for each day including its index. The sixth creates a moving average by averaging prices over a window defined by the current index. The seventh groups prices into weekly blocks of five indices. The eighth finds the day index of the largest single-day drop. The entry function coordinates these financial analyses. For example, an input of [100, 90, 110] returns a tuple containing the index one for the price drop, the cumulative returns, the formatted financial strings, and other portfolio results.

title: Aviation Altitude Tracker
spec: Implement an entry function `track(altitudes)` taking a list of flight altitudes. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the minute indices of all altitudes below ten thousand feet. The second calculates a cumulative altitude change up to each minute index. The third applies a sensor drift correction by adding the minute index to each altitude. The fourth identifies turbulence by comparing each altitude with the preceding and following minute indices. The fifth formats a flight log string for each minute including its index. The sixth creates an estimated trajectory by shifting altitudes forward by five minute indices. The seventh groups altitudes into hourly blocks of sixty indices. The eighth finds the minute index of the absolute highest altitude. The entry function returns a tuple of the flight metrics. For example, an input of [15000, 9000, 12000] returns a tuple containing the index one for the low altitude, the cumulative changes, the flight log strings, and other tracking results.

title: Warehouse Inventory Auditor
spec: Implement an entry function `audit(levels)` taking a list of daily inventory levels. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the day numbers of all levels below a restock threshold. The second calculates a cumulative holding cost up to each day index. The third applies a shrinkage factor by subtracting the day number from each level. The fourth identifies anomalous drops by comparing each level with the preceding and following day indices. The fifth formats an inventory report string for each day including its index. The sixth creates a restock schedule by projecting levels forward by three day indices. The seventh groups levels into weekly blocks of seven indices. The eighth finds the day index of the absolute lowest inventory. The entry function aggregates these inventory audits into a tuple. For example, an input of [50, 10, 40] returns a tuple containing the index one for the low inventory, the cumulative holding costs, the inventory report strings, and other audit results.

title: Water Quality Evaluator
spec: Implement an entry function `assess(readings)` taking a list of daily purity readings. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the day numbers of all readings below standard. The second calculates a cumulative purity average up to each day index. The third applies a sensor degradation curve by subtracting a fraction of the day number from each reading. The fourth identifies contamination events by comparing each reading with the preceding and following day indices. The fifth formats a quality report string for each day including its index. The sixth creates a forecast by shifting readings forward by four day indices. The seventh groups readings into monthly blocks of thirty indices. The eighth finds the day index of the absolute highest purity. The entry function returns a tuple of the water quality assessments. For example, an input of [99, 85, 95] returns a tuple containing the index one for the low purity, the cumulative averages, the quality report strings, and other assessment results.

title: Power Consumption Profiler
spec: Implement an entry function `profile(usage)` taking a list of hourly energy usages. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the hour indices of all usages exceeding peak threshold. The second calculates a cumulative energy total up to each hour index. The third applies a dynamic tariff by multiplying the usage by the hour index. The fourth identifies power surges by comparing each usage with the preceding and following hour indices. The fifth formats an energy report string for each hour including its index. The sixth creates a predictive load by shifting usages forward by twelve hour indices. The seventh groups usages into daily blocks of twenty four indices. The eighth finds the hour index of the absolute lowest usage. The entry function evaluates these energy metrics and returns them in a tuple. For example, an input of [100, 500, 200] returns a tuple containing the index one for the peak usage, the cumulative totals, the energy report strings, and other load results.

title: Social Media Feed Moderator
spec: Implement an entry function `moderate(posts)` taking a list of post strings. Write eight helper functions. The first finds the indices of all posts containing banned words. The second calculates a cumulative engagement score using the post length multiplied by its index. The third applies a shadowban by clearing the text of every tenth post based on its index. The fourth identifies duplicate posts by comparing each post with the preceding and following indices. The fifth formats a moderation report string for each post including its index. The sixth creates a chronological feed by prefixing each post with a timestamp derived from its index. The seventh groups posts into pages of twenty indices. The eighth finds the index of the longest post. The entry function returns all moderation results in a tuple. For example, an input of ["good post", "banned post"] returns a tuple containing the index one for the banned word, the engagement scores, the moderation report strings, and other feed results.

title: Movie Production Budgeter
spec: The entry function `budget(categories)` accepts a tuple containing eight lists of numbers representing daily costs for salaries, materials, locations, permits, catering, transport, marketing, and insurance. The function must return a tuple of eight new lists or values computed from the inputs. For salaries, multiply each cost by its position index plus one. For materials, add the position index multiplied by ten to each cost. For locations, subtract the position index from each cost. For permits, multiply each cost by its position index modulo three. For catering, add fifty to the cost if its position index is even. For transport, multiply the cost by two if its position index is exactly three or four. For marketing, add the square of the position index to each cost. For insurance, subtract five times the position index from each cost. Example: given eight lists each containing a single ten, the output tuple contains lists evaluated at position zero, producing ten for salaries, ten for materials, ten for locations, zero for permits, sixty for catering, ten for transport, ten for marketing, and ten for insurance.

title: Amusement Park Evaluator
spec: The entry function `evaluate(metrics)` receives a tuple of eight lists containing daily visitor counts for rollercoasters, water rides, carousels, drop towers, haunted houses, bumper cars, ferris wheels, and parades. It returns a tuple of eight newly processed lists or calculated values. For rollercoasters, multiply each count by its day index. For water rides, add one hundred to the count if the day index is odd. For carousels, subtract the day index from the count. For drop towers, multiply the count by the day index modulo four. For haunted houses, add the square of the day index to the count. For bumper cars, multiply the count by three if the day index is exactly zero. For ferris wheels, add twenty times the day index to the count. For parades, subtract the day index divided by two from the count. Example: evaluating eight lists each containing the number twenty yields a tuple starting with zero for rollercoasters and ending with twenty for parades, based on the rules for index zero.

title: Academic Transcript Formatter
spec: The entry function `format(records)` takes a tuple of eight lists of strings representing course names, grades, teacher names, extracurriculars, awards, absences, disciplinary actions, and comments. It returns a tuple of eight processed results. For course names, append the position index enclosed in parentheses to each name. For grades, return the position index of the first letter F found. For teacher names, prefix each name with its position index and a dot. For extracurriculars, return a list keeping only the strings located at even position indices. For awards, create a dictionary mapping the position index to the award string. For absences, return a list of tuples containing the position index and the date string. For disciplinary actions, return the position index of the last string in the list. For comments, truncate each string to a character length equal to its position index plus five.

title: Software Deployment Auditor
spec: The entry function `audit(logs)` accepts a tuple of eight lists representing commits, builds, tests, dependencies, linting, migrations, approvals, and rollbacks. The function returns a tuple of eight distinct analytical results. For commits, return a dictionary mapping the sequence index to the commit string. For builds, find and return the sequence index of the first build time integer exceeding one hundred. For tests, format each item into a string combining the sequence index, a colon, and the test name. For dependencies, return a list filtering out any strings where the sequence index is a multiple of three. For linting, compute the sum of the sequence indices of all strings containing the word error. For migrations, return a list of tuples pairing the sequence index with the database name string. For approvals, find the sequence index of the first string equaling rejected. For rollbacks, append a space and the sequence index to each reason string.

title: Botanical Garden Cataloger
spec: The entry function `catalog(zones)` takes a tuple of eight lists of plant name strings for tropical, desert, temperate, tundra, aquatic, alpine, carnivorous, and medicinal zones. It returns a tuple of eight processed lists or values. For the tropical list, map each plant name to its position index in a dictionary. For the desert list, find the position index of the first string equaling cactus. For the temperate list, append a hyphen and the position index to each plant name. For the tundra list, return a new list keeping only plants at odd position indices. For the aquatic list, return the position index of the longest plant name string. For the alpine list, prefix each name with its position index and a colon. For the carnivorous list, count how many plants have a character length exactly equal to their position index. For the medicinal list, return a list of tuples pairing the plant name with its position index. Example: a desert list starting with fern then cactus will return an index of one for the second result.

title: Restaurant Menu Optimizer
spec: The entry function `optimize(courses)` receives a tuple of eight lists of integer prices for appetizers, soups, salads, mains, sides, desserts, beverages, and specials. It returns a tuple of eight updated price lists or metrics. For appetizers, increase each price by its position index. For soups, return the position index of the highest price. For salads, subtract the position index from each price. For mains, multiply each price by its position index. For sides, return a list keeping only prices located at position indices less than five. For desserts, format a string for each item combining the position index, a space, and the price. For beverages, find the position index of the first price under ten. For specials, calculate the sum of all prices that are located at even position indices. Example: a mains list of ten, twenty, and thirty will return zero, twenty, and sixty.

title: Astronomy Observation Planner
spec: The entry function `plan(targets)` takes a tuple of eight lists of celestial object strings categorizing planets, moons, asteroids, comets, nebulae, galaxies, quasars, and pulsars. It returns a tuple of eight processed results. For planets, append the observation hour which equals the position index to each string. For moons, create a dictionary mapping the position index to the moon name. For asteroids, find the position index of the first string containing the letter x. For comets, filter the list to keep only targets at position indices two, three, five, and seven. For nebulae, format each string by enclosing the position index in brackets before the name. For galaxies, return a list of tuples containing the position index and the name. For quasars, find the position index of the longest string. For pulsars, return a single string joining all names using their position index as a separator. Example: a galaxies list of milky way yields a tuple containing zero and milky way.

title: Historical Timeline Builder
spec: The entry function `build(eras)` takes a tuple of eight lists of historical event strings spanning prehistory, antiquity, the middle ages, the renaissance, the industrial age, the modern age, the contemporary age, and the future. It returns a tuple of eight outputs. For prehistory, return a list of tuples pairing the event with its sequence index. For antiquity, create a dictionary mapping the event name to its sequence index multiplied by one hundred. For the middle ages, prefix each event with its sequence index and a dash. For the renaissance, find the sequence index of the first event containing the word art. For the industrial age, keep only events located at odd sequence indices. For the modern age, append a colon and the sequence index to each event string. For the contemporary age, return the sequence index of the shortest event description. For the future, create a dictionary with the sequence index as the key and the event as the value.

title: Cybersecurity Threat Analyzer
spec: The entry function `analyze(streams)` accepts a tuple of eight lists of network packet strings classified as malware, phishing, denial of service, intrusions, exploits, botnets, spam, and ransomware. It returns a tuple of eight extracted metrics. For malware, find the sequence index of the first packet containing the word evil. For phishing, create a dictionary mapping the sequence index to the packet string. For denial of service, filter the list to keep only packets where the sequence index is a multiple of ten. For intrusions, format each packet by prepending the sequence index and a warning label. For exploits, return a list of tuples pairing the sequence index with the packet string. For botnets, count how many packets have a sequence index matching their character length. For spam, return the sequence index of the last packet in the list. For ransomware, append the sequence index to each packet string to represent an encryption key.

title: Video Game Level Designer
spec: The entry function `design(elements)` receives a tuple of eight lists of strings representing enemies, obstacles, powerups, checkpoints, secrets, coins, bosses, and backgrounds. It returns a tuple of eight processed collections. For enemies, create a dictionary mapping the enemy type to its spawn sequence index. For obstacles, return the sequence index of the first string equaling spike. For powerups, append the sequence index to each powerup name. For checkpoints, return a list filtering out strings at even sequence indices. For secrets, format each as a string starting with the sequence index followed by the secret location. For coins, return a list of tuples containing the sequence index and the coin string. For bosses, find the sequence index of the string with the most uppercase letters. For backgrounds, join all strings together using their sequence index as a delimiter. Example: an obstacles list with pit then spike returns an index of one.

title: Urban Planning Simulator
spec: The entry function `simulate(districts)` receives a tuple of eight lists of integers representing population counts for residential, commercial, industrial, parks, schools, hospitals, transit, and entertainment zones. It returns a tuple of eight calculated outputs. For residential zones, multiply each population by its district index. For commercial zones, return the district index of the highest population. For industrial zones, create a dictionary mapping the district index to the population divided by ten. For parks, filter out populations where the district index is less than three. For schools, format a string for each district combining the district index and the student count. For hospitals, return a list of tuples of the district index and the bed capacity. For transit zones, count how many districts have a population exactly equal to their district index. For entertainment zones, calculate the sum of the populations located at odd district indices.

title: Music Festival Organizer
spec: The entry function `organize(stages)` takes a tuple of eight lists of artist name strings for the main, acoustic, electronic, rock, jazz, indie, hip hop, and comedy stages. It returns a tuple of eight processed outputs. For the main stage, append the performance slot index to each artist name. For the acoustic stage, find the slot index of the first artist whose name contains no spaces. For the electronic stage, create a dictionary mapping the slot index to a beats per minute integer calculated as the slot index times ten plus one hundred. For the rock stage, filter out artists located at slot indices divisible by three. For the jazz stage, format a string announcing the slot index and the artist. For the indie stage, return a list of tuples with the slot index and the artist. For the hip hop stage, find the slot index of the artist with the longest name. For the comedy tent, create a dictionary linking the slot index to the performer string.

title: Property Asset Allocator
spec: The entry function `allocate(properties)` receives a tuple of eight lists of integer values for apartments, houses, condos, townhomes, commercial spaces, land, industrial sites, and retail units. It returns a tuple of eight financial summaries. For apartments, increase each value by a percentage equal to its position index. For houses, find the position index of the first value exceeding one million. For condos, create a dictionary mapping the position index to a maintenance fee calculated as the value divided by one hundred. For townhomes, filter out values located at even position indices. For commercial spaces, format a ledger string combining the position index and the value. For land, return a list of tuples pairing the position index with the value. For industrial sites, find the position index of the lowest value. For retail units, calculate the sum of all values located at position indices greater than five.

title: Emergency Room Coordinator
spec: The entry function `coordinate(departments)` accepts a tuple of eight lists of patient surnames for trauma, pediatrics, cardiology, neurology, oncology, orthopedics, radiology, and pharmacy. It returns a tuple of eight organizational lists or metrics. For trauma, append the triage sequence index to each surname. For pediatrics, find the sequence index of the first patient named Smith. For cardiology, create a dictionary mapping the sequence index to the surname. For neurology, filter out patients located at sequence indices that are multiples of four. For oncology, format a wristband string with the sequence index and the surname. For orthopedics, return a list of tuples of the sequence index and the surname. For radiology, find the sequence index of the shortest surname. For pharmacy, create a dictionary of the sequence index as the key and a generated prescription ID string as the value.

title: Aircraft Maintenance Scheduler
